prompt: Which of these writes are idempotent? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: SET qty = 98
choices.why: Yes: a second run sets the same value.

choices.text: SET qty = qty - 2
choices.why: Each run subtracts again.

choices.text: INSERT the sale keyed by its id, ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
choices.why: Yes: the second copy has nowhere to go.

choices.text: Append a line to a log file
choices.why: Each run adds a line.

choices.text: Write a file at a fixed name with the same content
choices.why: Yes: the second write leaves the same file.

prompt: The table holds bk-04 with qty 0. `UPDATE sold SET qty = qty + 2` runs twice for the same sale. What is qty now?
Why can a payment API not simply be made idempotent the way the sales table was?

choices.text: You do not control the shape of its write
choices.why: Right. Then the consumer has to remember what it has done.

choices.text: Payments are too fast to be stored in a table
choices.why: Speed is not the issue; who controls the write is.

choices.text: Kafka cannot carry payment events
choices.why: It carries any bytes; the problem is downstream.

choices.text: Payment APIs have primary keys that are too long for SQLite
choices.why: The API is not a table at all.

prompt: The sink writes the sale's id to `processed` in one transaction and updates the stock in a second one. What does a crash between them cause?

choices.text: The sale is applied twice on the next delivery
choices.why: That is the other order; here the id is already recorded.

choices.text: Nothing, because the id makes it safe
choices.why: Only if both share a transaction.

choices.text: A sale marked as applied that never was
choices.why: Right. The next delivery skips it, and the stock never moves.

choices.text: SQLite refuses the second transaction
choices.why: Nothing refuses it; the process is simply gone.

prompt: Why is the Kafka offset not a good id to deduplicate sales by?

choices.text: Offsets change when a topic is compacted
choices.why: Offsets never change; compaction leaves gaps.

choices.text: One sale retried sits at two offsets
choices.why: Right. The id has to come from the event.

choices.text: Offsets are too large to store
choices.why: They are one integer each.

choices.text: Two partitions cannot have the same offset
choices.why: They can and do; that is a separate problem.

choices.text: One number per partition, not one per event
choices.why: Right. And it needs no window, because it never grows.

choices.text: SQLite stores and compares integers faster than it does text
choices.why: A real difference, but not the one that matters.

choices.text: It lets Kafka do the deduplication on the broker instead
choices.why: Kafka is not involved; the database decides where to start.

choices.text: It needs no transaction
choices.why: It needs one: effect and offset together.

prompt: A team deletes processed ids older than seven days. Which duplicate can still get through?

choices.text: A producer retry after a lost acknowledgement
choices.why: That arrives within seconds.

choices.text: A redelivery after a rebalance
choices.why: Seconds again.

choices.text: A crash that the consumer recovers from in an hour
choices.why: An hour is well inside seven days.

choices.text: A replay of the topic from a month ago
choices.why: Right. Those ids were forgotten, so the sales are applied again.

choices.text: Version 3's

choices.text: Version 1's, since it came first

choices.text: None; SQLite refuses the conflict

Why is the event's timestamp a weak version?

choices.text: Timestamps take too much space
choices.why: They are eight bytes.

choices.text: SQLite cannot compare timestamps
choices.why: It can; the problem is what they mean.

choices.text: Kafka rewrites timestamps on every topic
choices.why: Only LogAppendTime topics replace them.

choices.text: Clocks tie and disagree
choices.why: Right. Lesson 9's clocks disagree more than people expect.

prompt: Why does the outbox pattern write the event into a table of the same database?

choices.text: So the change and its event commit together or not at all
choices.why: Right. One of the two systems leaves the moment that matters.

choices.text: Because Kafka cannot be reached from the program
choices.why: The relay reaches it; the point is atomicity.

choices.text: To make the event smaller
choices.why: The payload is the same.

choices.text: So that the relay never sends an event twice
choices.why: The relay delivers at least once; duplicates are handled by the id.

prompt: The relay crashes after Kafka acknowledged two events and before marking them sent. What happens next?

choices.text: They are lost
choices.why: They are still unsent in the table.

choices.text: The database rolls back the restock
choices.why: The restock committed long before.

choices.text: They are sent again, with the same ids
choices.why: Right. Consumers deduplicate by the id made at the change.

choices.text: Kafka refuses them because idempotence is on
choices.why: A new relay run is a new producer session.

prompt: An outbox relay delivers each event at least ___, which is why every event carries an id.
What does the duplicate test compare?

choices.text: The topic's size before and after
choices.why: The topic does not change; the output might.

choices.text: The consumer's output after one run and after a second run over the same input
choices.why: Right. If the second run changes anything, the consumer is not idempotent.

choices.text: The consumer group's lag
choices.why: Lag says how far behind, not whether effects repeat.

choices.text: The number of lines each run prints to the terminal, which should match from one run to the next
choices.why: Both runs print a line; the output data is what matters.

prompt: A sink keeps per-shop daily totals by adding each sale's cents. It must survive replays from any point in the topic's retention. Which design fits best?

choices.text: Keep processed ids for one day
choices.why: A replay from last week gets through.

choices.text: Switch the producer to idempotent
choices.why: That does nothing for replays or the consumer's gap.

choices.text: Store the sales keyed by id and compute totals from them
choices.why: Right. An idempotent write needs no memory and no window.

choices.text: Commit offsets after every single sale instead of after every batch
choices.why: That shrinks crash duplicates, not replays.
